questions.q: Who was the chairman of the Drafting Committee responsible for preparing the Constitution?
questions.a: The chairman was Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. A wrong answer here suggests the student has not memorized the primary leadership figures mentioned in the historical record of the Assembly.

questions.q: Why did India need a Constitution immediately after becoming independent?
questions.a: India needed a Constitution to set up a stable government structure and protect the rights of its people. A wrong answer (e.g., "to make laws for the British") shows a failure to understand that the Constitution replaced colonial rule with a new, independent legal framework.

questions.q: If you were part of the Constituent Assembly, why would it be important to have members from different regions and religions?
questions.a: Steps: 1. Identify the goal of unity. 2. Recognize that India is diverse. 3. Realize that laws must represent everyone to be fair. 4. Conclude that diverse representation prevents one group from dominating others. This shows the student understands the principle of inclusivity in democracy.

questions.q: How did the number of members in the Constituent Assembly change from 1946 to the final drafting period?
questions.a: The number dropped from 389 to 299 due to the partition of India. A wrong answer indicates a lack of awareness of the historical context surrounding the timeline of the Assembly.

questions.q: Is the Constitution a static document that never changes? (Based on the scope provided, judge the need for a structure).
questions.a: No, it is a document that provides the structure for the country, though we are not focusing on how it changes here. It is a foundational framework for governance. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks it is just a historical relic rather than a living, active framework.

questions.q: Imagine you are writing a "Constitution" for your classroom. What are the first three things you would include to ensure everyone is treated fairly?
questions.a: A good answer includes: 1. A rule for choosing a class monitor (government structure), 2. A list of student rights (like freedom to speak), and 3. A rule for resolving arguments (justice). A poor answer lists arbitrary rules like "no homework," which ignores the concept of governance.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The ______ is the fundamental rulebook of a country that defines how the government works and guarantees the basic rights of its citizens.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are starting a new sports club with fifty friends, but you have no rules—______ would argue about how to play or who gets to lead.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to identify the purpose of the Constitution and describe the role of the Constituent Assembly and the Drafting Committee in its creation.
